title: Downtown Cary Park Hosts Its First Diwali Celebration on the Great Lawn
excerpt: The Town of Cary staged its first Diwali celebration at Downtown Cary Park on Monday evening, with dance, drumming and opening remarks from Councilmember Sarika Bansal.
body:
• Downtown Cary Park hosted its first Diwali celebration on Monday, October 26, from 6:30 to 8 p.m. at the Great Lawn Pavilion.
  • Councilmember Sarika Bansal opened the program; Ishana Dance Co, Dhol Tasha and Leela Dance Co performed, with Arunima Das as emcee and music by DJ Rang.
  • The town-hosted event was free and open to the public at 327 S. Academy Street, with lawn seating — attendees brought their own chairs and blankets.
  • It joins Hum Sub Diwali, the Triangle's largest Diwali festival, in Cary's festival season, ahead of Diwali's main day on Sunday, November 8, 2026.

Downtown Cary Park hosted its first Diwali celebration on Monday evening, as the Town of Cary brought the Festival of Lights to the Great Lawn Pavilion for an evening of dance, drumming and community programming. The free event ran from 6:30 to 8 p.m. at the park at 327 S. Academy Street, giving Cary a town-run Diwali celebration of its own in the town's flagship downtown park.

An Evening on the Great Lawn

Councilmember Sarika Bansal opened the program with remarks, according to the event details published by Triangle on the Cheap. The stage lineup featured performances by Ishana Dance Co, the Dhol Tasha drum ensemble and Leela Dance Co, hosted by emcee Arunima Das. DJ Rang played music before and after the performances, and attendees set up their own chairs and blankets on the lawn for the show.

The park's own event listing described the evening as a chance to "experience an evening of music, dance, and community as we celebrate the Festival of Lights together," with performances and activities held at the Great Lawn Pavilion. Food was part of the billing alongside the music and dance.

A Different Scale From Hum Sub Diwali

Cary is not new to Diwali. Hum Sub Diwali, the community festival at Koka Booth Amphitheatre, ran a full day of programming on Saturday, October 10, from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., with daytime cultural performances, a formal inauguration and lamp lighting at noon, an exhibition on Indian cinema, food and artisan vendors, and a fireworks finale over Symphony Lake at 9 p.m. Triangle on the Cheap describes Hum Sub Diwali as the largest Diwali celebration in the Triangle.

Monday's park celebration was a different format: ninety minutes in the early evening, hosted by the town itself rather than a community organization, and staged in a municipal park in the middle of downtown. Where Hum Sub is a destination festival that draws the region to an amphitheatre, the park event put Diwali on the regular calendar of a public space Cary residents already use for concerts, movie nights and farmers markets.

Why a Town-Hosted Celebration Matters

For Indian American families in Cary and across the western Wake County suburbs, Diwali has traditionally been marked at home, at temples and at community-run festivals. A celebration staged by the town, in the town's central park, and opened by a member of the Town Council places the festival alongside the park's other civic programming. The listing framed the evening as one for the whole town, not only for families who observe the holiday at home — an invitation to neighbors of every background to watch the performances and learn what the festival marks.

That framing fits the festival itself. Diwali is observed across Hindu, Jain, Sikh and some Buddhist traditions, each attaching the lamps to a different story, and public celebrations in American suburbs have become one of the main ways the wider community encounters it.

What's Next

The park celebration landed ahead of Diwali itself. The festival's main day in 2026, the night of Lakshmi Puja, falls on Sunday, November 8, with the five-day observance opening on Dhanteras, Friday, November 6. Families across the Triangle marking the festival at home will light diyas through that weekend. Whether the park celebration returns next year has not been announced; the park's fall programming continues on its published calendar.
